interactions.summary: Jiang gives his explicit answer that both hell and purgatory are chosen through free will, then the reading immediately reinforces the theme with penitents whose pride has been reinterpreted as humility, service, and the emptiness of worldly glory.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led exchange followed by quoted reading

claims.claim: Jiang's core claim is that people are in hell because they choose that condition and people are in purgatory because they choose the path of becoming better; the same suffering changes meaning through free will and attitude.
Jiang names the difference between hell and purgatory as punishment versus opportunity, which is why growth mindset belongs to the latter.
The reading of Umberto and Odorisi supplies Dantean evidence that pride is cured by humiliation, service, and a recognition that artistic and worldly fame quickly decay.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses Dante's anthropology into a stark formula: hell is experienced as punishment, purgatory as opportunity.
signature_moments.source_phrase: people in hell see it as their punishment, but people in puritory see it as their opportunity
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the lecture's most portable statement of the free-will distinction.

signature_moments.moment: Worldly renown is reduced to wind that changes name as it changes course.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Worldly renown is nothing other than a breath of wind
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The reading gives a poetic image for why pride must be purged.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Free will is Jiang's explanation for why identical outer punishment can become either damnation or purification depending on what the soul chooses it to mean.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture moves from student hypotheses to Jiang's explicit doctrinal answer about free will, then confirms it through the terrace-of-pride reading.
